scribe_response.text: What was a typical day like in your working life? A normal day at work started very early, while, while it was still dark. I lived a long way off then and took the first bus with the milk men. I arrived at Saint Aldric's by six, and the night staff were grey um with tiredness. We sat in the ward kitchen with strong tea and a plate of toast for the handover. The night sister read out each patient from a battered notebook, um bed by bed. I wrote it all on a bit of paper and put it in um my pocket. By um half past six the lights were on, and the um day began. The ward was long, with twenty-eight beds and tall windows down both sides. The floor was shiny, and you, and you could hear anyone walking from the far end. First came the bedpans and washing, with bowls of warm um water carried on trays. Every bed was stripped a- and done again properly, and I checked each one. A crooked sheet meant a crooked day, as far as I was um concerned. Food came on a trolley with big tins, tins of uh tea and porridge and bread. Those who could sit up ate at a table, and I sat with the grumpy ones. What happened next? After that there was the round with the trolley and the keys that jangled. I counted the tablets into little cups, and two of us had to sign. At nine, At nine the doctors came in a, a group, with the important one at the front. I walked beside him with the charts and told him honestly what the night had been like. Later um in the morning there were wounds to do and things to put up on poles. I used a tray of tools and, and um bandages, and my hands um never shook. At eleven the tea came, uh and the whole room seemed to relax. Dinner at noon was minced beef, mashed potato and boiled swede. I tried it myself every day, because you uh cannot complain if you have not tried it. Visiting began at two, uh and the relatives arrived with flowers, grapes uh and nervous faces. A man who used to make furniture was ill in my ward one winter. He gave me a present that he had made um himself, a small, a small bird. I think he did um it because it was a special day for me. Now it sits in my uh kitchen by, kitchen by the window. I stood at the door and spoke to each family, um because nobody should go in alone. Can you tell me more about that? In the afternoon, afternoon the young ones came, and I showed them things. I told them, them that it was like talking, and they should um listen. At three something always went wrong, um like a fall or a faint or a blocked thing. We dealt with it, and nobody outside ever knew how close it was. The big boss came round at four in her stiff hat, hat, and everyone stood up straight. She uh ran a finger along the window and looked at it, and said nothing. At six uh the evening staff arrived, and I handed over, bed by bed, from my own slip of paper. Before I left, I uh walked round again and said goodnight to each person. Mister um Jenkins in uh bed fourteen always held up two fingers, meaning he was alive and um cross. I went home on the bus with sore feet and my head full of names. My husband had made something for dinner, nothing special, but I thought it was lovely. Helen would be doing her homework at the uh kitchen table with h- her tongue between her teeth. I put my feet in a bowl and read the paper for a bit. Then I slept like a stone and got up early to do it all again. It was hard work and tiring, but I would not change a minute of it.
